I have been farming this land in Quzhou County for over forty years. Here on the North China Plain, the weather and soil are made for the wheat-maize double crop rotation, and that is what I have always done. I cannot read or write, but I know the seasons by heart, and I watch what my neighbors do. I have about eight mu of good flat land. In October, I will rotary till the fields and sow winter wheat using improved seeds — varieties like the ones my neighbors grow that handle the winter cold and give steady yields. I will put down compound fertilizer as a basal dressing and topdress with nitrogen when the wheat starts to green up and at jointing. I will irrigate three or four times, especially at the critical stages, and spray for weeds, insects, and disease about four times through the season.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will immediately sow summer maize using hybrid seeds — the kind that gives the best yield around here. I will not till the soil again; I will just sow directly into the wheat stubble to save time and fuel before the summer rains. The maize needs less fertilizer than the wheat, and I will irrigate it twice and spray pesticides three or four times to keep the pests away. This rotation feeds my family, and any surplus I can sell at the village market. It is the way my father farmed, and it is the way I will farm this year.

decision.reasoning_summary: I follow the traditional winter wheat–summer maize double cropping rotation on my 8 mu of land in Quzhou County, which is standard for the North China Plain and ensures both family food security and market sales. I use rotary tillage for wheat in autumn and no-tillage for maize sown directly after the June wheat harvest to save labor and fuel. I apply compound and urea fertilizers based on local practice, irrigate wheat four times and maize twice, and spray pesticides several times per crop to manage weeds, insects, and diseases. These decisions reflect what I have learned from decades of farming and observing my neighbors.
